History of the Russian Revolution (HIST 1313)

How do you pull off a revolution? How do you stage a coup, and how does power actually change hands? What makes a change of regime revolutionary in the first place? Is any new government enough, or does it take something more? This course puts those questions to one of the defining upheavals of the modern world. We start by asking when the Russian Revolution really began. Some trace it all the way back to the Great Reforms of the 1860s. We’ll move briskly through that background, pick up speed with the Revolution of 1905, and then slow way down for the pivotal years of 1917 and 1918. World War I and the Civil War get equal billing, carrying us through 1920. And when did it end? By some measures, only with the destruction of the peasantry in the collectivization drives of the 1930s, so we’ll close with a quick run through the 1920s and beyond. You’ll have to decide for yourself. Throughout the course, beginnings, endings, and the balance of continuity and change stay open questions for you to argue.

What sets this course apart is where it looks. Petrograd, Lenin, Trotsky, Stalin and company all make their appearances, but they share the stage. We’ll treat 1917 as a pan-Eurasian story of total imperial collapse: a whole cluster of revolutions, unfolding from Central Asia and the Caucasus to Ukraine, Mongolia, and northern Iran, and spilling past the old empire’s borders into short-lived soviet republics in Hungary and Bavaria. Along the way you’ll meet anarchist peasant armies, Muslim reformers turned Bolsheviks, a Menshevik republic in Georgia, and a Baltic German baron who dreamed of restoring the empire of Chinggis Khan. We’ll also take up the people the capital-centered story tends to sideline, especially women and the peasants, and approach this as a peasant revolution first and foremost. Finally, we’ll place 1917 in a longer arc that runs from the Enlightenment and the French Revolution, through the world the communist twentieth century built, to the present, where the revolution’s legacy is still a live political argument.
